questions.q: What is the formula for the memory a full-precision classical simulator needs to store an n-qubit state vector, and why?
options: 2^n × 16 bytes, because the state has 2^n complex amplitudes and each one is typically stored as two 8-byte doubles (real + imaginary)
n × 16 bytes, because memory scales linearly with the number of qubits
2^n × 2 bytes, because each amplitude is a single bit flag
16 bytes total, regardless of n, because only the current measurement result needs to be stored
questions.explain: An n-qubit state vector has 2^n amplitudes (one per basis state), and each complex amplitude needs two 8-byte doubles — 16 bytes — giving a total of 2^n × 16 bytes, which the lesson computed directly rather than assumed.

questions.q: According to the real node-computed table in the lesson, roughly where does a state-vector simulation cross from 'fits on a laptop' into 'needs a serious compute cluster'?
options: Somewhere around n=30 (16 GB) to n=40 (16 TB) qubits
Around n=5 qubits
It never crosses that line — simulators scale fine to any number of qubits
Exactly at n=100 qubits
questions.explain: The computed table showed n=24 at 256 MB (laptop-friendly), n=30 at 16 GB (high-end consumer machine), and n=40 already at 16 TB, which requires a serious cluster — each additional 10 qubits multiplies the requirement by roughly 1,024×.

questions.q: Why can't a cleverer simulator algorithm (such as the index-pairing gate-application technique from the previous lesson) fix the exponential memory problem?
options: Because the problem is about the size of the state vector itself (2^n amplitudes, a property of what an n-qubit state fundamentally is), not about how efficiently any single gate is applied to it
Because JavaScript specifically cannot handle large arrays
Because index-pairing actually makes memory usage worse, not better
Because the problem only exists for the Hadamard gate
questions.explain: Index-pairing makes applying a gate efficient by avoiding a full 2^n × 2^n matrix, but it still has to read and write all 2^n amplitudes in the state array — it cannot shrink the array itself, because a general n-qubit state genuinely has that many independent amplitudes.

questions.q: Why does a real quantum computer with n physical qubits avoid paying the 2^n memory cost that a classical simulator pays?
options: Because the hardware physically IS in the superposition across that 2^n-dimensional space as a direct consequence of quantum mechanics, rather than having to explicitly store a list of 2^n numbers somewhere
Because quantum computers use a more efficient classical memory chip
Because quantum computers only ever use a small number of amplitudes at once
Because quantum computers round all amplitudes to fewer decimal places
questions.explain: A real quantum computer's n qubits simply are in a joint superposition state as a physical fact — there is no explicit memory array being maintained, unlike a classical simulator which must track every one of the 2^n amplitudes explicitly in RAM.

questions.q: The lesson connects the exponential wall back to Chapter 1's warning against the 'tries all answers at once' myth. What is the precise connection?
options: A real quantum computer accesses an exponentially large state space 'for free,' but still only yields n classical bits on measurement and still needs a specific algorithm to make the right answer's probability dominant before that measurement — the exponential advantage is in representation, not in automatic readout
The exponential wall proves that quantum computers are strictly slower than classical ones for every problem
There is no real connection; the two ideas are unrelated facts covered in different chapters
The exponential wall means quantum computers can read out all 2^n amplitudes directly, bypassing the need for algorithms entirely
questions.explain: The resource gap explains why quantum hardware is worth building at all (classical simulation becomes impossible past ~40-50 qubits), but Chapter 1 already established that having access to an exponential state space does not by itself solve anything — a useful algorithm still has to engineer which outcomes are likely before the single classical measurement collapses everything.
